en: An Eulogy on the *Buddhabhāṣita-prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, composed by the Śramaṇa Ce.

In preparing to explain this sūtra, I shall analyze it according to four sections: first, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, the discernment of the sūtra’s central tenet.
The body [of this work] consists of: first, the general introduction; second, the purpose of the treatise; third, the explanation of the title;

and fourth, the critical analysis and commentary of the text. Regarding the arising of the teaching: I humbly observe that the ultimate truth is profound and tranquil, wondrously transcending the realms of existence and non-existence. The characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are exceedingly deep, able to surpass the sphere of names and words. Nevertheless, as there is no fixed method for approaching this truth, the doctrine of the two *piṭakas* was opened; and as the establishment of the teaching must have a basis, the manifestations of the three bodies (*trikāya*) were fully revealed. This may be likened to clear spring water wherein the moon’s reflection suddenly appears, or to the celestial drum sounding spontaneously when all enemies move in secret darkness.

Thus, responding to beings occurs at the appropriate time, and guidance is provided according to their capacities; this is why the Tathāgata preached the three wheels of Dharma. For those who had not yet entered the Dharma, he caused them to enter it; thus, in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, he first expounded the causes and effects of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—this was the first wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, which is able to eliminate the grasping at a self.

For those who had already entered, he turned them toward the Mahāyāna; on Vulture Peak and in fifteen other assemblies, he taught the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras—this is the second wheel of signless Dharma. Through this, the grasping at phenomena as having intrinsic nature is gradually severed, yet the grasping at emptiness itself has still not been dispelled.

Therefore, within the pure and impure lands such as the third Lotus Treasury World, the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other definitive Mahāyāna sūtras were taught; these fully reveal the two principles of emptiness and existence, simultaneously eliminating the two biased attachments to existence and non-existence. This is the emergence of the teaching.

Regarding the term "essence of the tenet" (*zongti*): "essence" generally clarifies the essence of the teaching that expresses [the truth], while "tenet" specifically reveals that which is expressed by the various teachings.

However, there are differing views concerning the essence of the Buddha's teaching; according to the Sarvāstivāda school, sound constitutes its essence, because names and so forth are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), whereas sound is virtuous (*kuśala*).
According to the Sautrāntika school, the continuum is a conventional designation of sound, because apart from sound there are no distinct names, phrases, and so forth.
According to the Mahāyāna school, the various teachings differ: in some instances it is sound alone, as in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, where in certain Buddha-fields sound constitutes the Buddha-work;
in other instances it takes names and so forth as its substance, as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, where the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena takes names and so forth as its objects.

In some instances, it is appropriate to speak of sound (*śabda*) and names (*nāman*), etc., as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Both the speaker and the listener rely upon two things, namely, sound and names, etc."

As for how there are such differences among the various teachings: in terms of ultimate reality, the conventional follows the real; all [dharmas] take sounds, names, and so forth as their essential nature. However, because each of the sacred teachings relies upon a specific aspect of meaning, they do not contradict one another.
Why is this so? Because when following the conventional from the ultimate, sound constitutes the substance, for apart from sound there are no distinct names, phrases, and so forth;

because when following the substantial from the functional, names and so forth constitute the substance, for they serve as the basis for the two types of expression—the self-nature and the specific qualities of all phenomena.
The provisional and the real depend upon one another; taken together, they are said to constitute the essence (*tattva*), for if either one were lacking, the explanation would not be complete.
When taking the object from the perspective of the mind, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is used as the essence, because the sūtras state that all phenomena are not separate from consciousness.
When subsuming the delusory into the true, suchness (*tathatā*) is used as the essence, because the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* and other texts speak of the nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

Regarding the tenets to be explained, there are briefly three types: first, tenets distinguished according to specific ailments; second, tenets revealed according to specific schools; and third, tenets distinguished according to time periods.

Regarding the distinct tenets according to specific ailments: it refers to the fact that all sentient beings, due to ignorance, give rise to eighty-four thousand gateways of affliction, such as greed and hatred. Therefore, the Tathāgata prescribes medicine according to the ailment, providing eighty-four thousand dharma-gateways such as the aggregates (*skandha*). Consequently, each of these, as appropriate to the case, takes the aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) as its expressed tenet.

Regarding the distinct doctrines of the various schools: although each school possesses its own various gateways, when one investigates their underlying intent, they are each distinct according to their respective tradition. For example, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* takes the One Vehicle as its doctrine; the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* takes non-duality as its doctrine; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* takes Buddha-nature as its doctrine; and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* takes the cause and fruit of the noble ones as its doctrine. All other schools should be understood accordingly based on these examples.

Regarding the identification of the tenets according to their periods: although the various categories of the holy teachings are numerous, when identifying the tenets according to their periods, they do not exceed three types. These three types are the Four Noble Truths, the Signless (animitta), and the definitive Mahāyāna, as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. Among these, this present treatise takes the Signless as its primary tenet.
Regarding the title of "The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom Spoken by the Buddha":

"Spoken by the Buddha" (Fo shuo) identifies the speaker. In the Indic language, *buddha* is translated here as "Awakened" (*jue*). Possessing both ultimate and conventional wisdom, and having perfected the awakening of both self and others, he is therefore called a Buddha.
To open and manifest the wondrous gate, causing sentient beings to understand it, is called "explaining.
Regarding "Prajñāpāramitā," this explains the dharma being taught; in this land, it is translated as "Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore."

The *Heart Sūtra* correctly reveals the teaching that expresses [the ultimate truth]. Within the path of the Way, the Sovereign Mind (citta-rāja) stands out preeminently; among all Prajñāpāramitā teachings, this scripture is the most honored. Its name is established based on this metaphor, and thus it is called "Heart" (hṛdaya).

The term *sūtra* has two meanings: "to pierce through" and "to hold together. It "pierces through" the meanings that ought to be explained and "holds together" those beings who are to be converted. This is thus a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Since the name is established based on both the means and the object of expression—the Dharma and the discourse—it is called the "Buddha-spoken Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom (*Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*)."
"Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
This is the fourth section, the explanatory commentary.

Within this sutra, there are three parts in total: first, the elucidation of the wisdom that contemplates; second, from "Śāriputra" onwards, the discernment of the object contemplated; and third, from "Because there is nothing to be apprehended" onwards, the manifestation of the fruit attained.

The reason there is no introduction or circulation section is that this work is a concise compilation of the essential points from among all the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras; therefore, it contains only the main body of the teaching, without an introduction or a circulation section.
It is like the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, which does not possess the three divisions [of introduction, main body, and circulation].

Regarding the term "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," it is further divided into two parts within the initial section: first, the designation of the person who performs the contemplation; second, the discernment of the essence of the contemplative wisdom. This [sentence] constitutes the first: the designation of the person who performs the contemplation.

If one follows the original name Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara), it was established based on the bodhisattva observing all worlds through the vocal karma of uttering the name to rescue beings from various calamities; thus, this title alone has not yet fully revealed the observation of his bodily and mental karmas.

Now, regarding the original text’s use of the term "Avalokiteśvara" (觀自在): internally he realizes the two kinds of emptiness, and externally he contemplates the three karmas; because he acts with spontaneous mastery without relying on deliberate effort, he is called Avalokiteśvara.
Now, this Bodhisattva is in reality at the stage of the cause, being one who will attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime; yet he is spoken of as having already attained Buddhahood.
Even if that were so, what fault would there be?
If he is indeed a Bodhisattva, how would you interpret and reconcile this?

In the *Avalokiteśvara Samādhi Sūtra*, it is said that the Buddha told Ānanda: "I now speak the truth; this matter is not false. I recall that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood before me, and was named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Buddha, Bhagavat, known as the Tathāgata Righteous Dharma Radiance."
At that time, I was a disciple practicing austerities under that Buddha.
If [the one who received the prediction] were that Buddha, how could one reconcile this with the prediction granted to Avalokiteśvara?
Therefore, that sūtra says: "Good son!..."
The lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas; yet it shall have its end, and he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he said: "O son of good family!"

After the True Dharma of Amitābha Buddha has ceased, past the middle watch of the night, at the time when the morning star appears, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara shall sit cross-legged beneath a bodhi tree made of the seven precious jewels and attain equal and perfect enlightenment, receiving the title Tathāgata Universal Radiance Mountain King of Merit, complete with the ten epithets, and even the name of his land, Adorned with Myriad Jewels.

Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states that Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara cultivates the bodhisattva practices in this land, and at the end of his life, he is reborn through transformation in that Buddha-land.
The commentary states: Because the name "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the same person despite appearing in different forms, the various accounts of him do not contradict one another.
This is like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, where all Buddhas share the same title, Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp).
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: Avalokiteśvara himself has two aspects: first, the real body; second, the transformation body.
The former is the real body, as described in the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*;
the latter is the transformation body, as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

As stated in the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, although Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained enlightenment long ago, he is said to have now become a Buddha from the perspective of his manifested form (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
Although there are two such interpretations, the latter is superior, as it accords with the various sacred teachings and does not contradict reason.
Regarding the phrase "when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*," this second section distinguishes the wisdom that contemplates.
Within it, there are two parts: first, clarifying the essence of wisdom; second, distinguishing the function of wisdom. This [section] distinguishes the essence of wisdom.
"Practice" (*caryā*) refers to proceeding; it is the wisdom capable of contemplation.
"Profound" (*gambhīra*) means extremely deep; there are two kinds of profundity. First, the profundity of practice itself:

non-conceptual wisdom internally realizes the two kinds of emptiness and is free from all conceptualization. Because it lacks the characteristics of practice consisting of a subject and an object of practice, it is called the profundity of practice. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Not seeing practice, not seeing non-practice—this is called the Bodhisattva practicing the profound Prajñā."

Second, the profundity of the object (*ālambana*), which refers to the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*). It is free from the marks of existence and non-existence and transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) realizes this profound object, it is called "profound practice."
The Sanskrit term "prajñā" is translated here as "wisdom.
The term "pāra" means "the other shore," and "mita" means "to reach.
Thus, it signifies reaching the other shore.

According to that [Sanskrit], it should be called "reaching the other shore through wisdom" (*prajñā-pāramitā*); from this perspective, however, it is termed "wisdom reaching the other shore. Because one reaches the city of Nirvāṇa by means of wisdom to sever the hindrances, it is therefore called "wisdom reaching the other shore."
"Time" refers to temporal divisions.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that time divisions are conventionally designated based on conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), yet time, number, and so forth are not included among the categories of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), or elements (*dhātu*).

The *Śramaṇaparivarta* provides the same explanation; thus that treatise states: "When time is designated as a conventional name based on phenomena (*dharma*), there is no separate time apart from those phenomena.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state that time is a provisional designation for the preceding and succeeding stages of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and that it is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) as a factor dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is also stated in this same way; thus that treatise says: "The establishment of non-associated temporal states, or mental images."

The general explanation of the intent is as follows: there are three types of *prajñā*, namely, the *prajñā* of words, the *prajñā* of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). In order to clarify the *prajñā* of contemplation and distinguish it from the *prajñā* of ultimate reality and the others, it is said that when one practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, these three types of *prajñā* should be explained therein.

"Clearly perceiving that the five aggregates are all empty" distinguishes the function of wisdom; this function is twofold: first, self-benefit, and second, benefiting others. This clarifies that contemplating emptiness is itself self-benefit.
In order to explain this text, I shall first set forth the various contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) and subsequently rely upon those prior contemplations to interpret the words of this sūtra.

Regarding the mention of "various contemplations," the Buddha-dharma is profoundly deep and fundamentally of a single flavor; yet because students have not yet realized this, divergent doctrines arise. Therefore, in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, the World-Honored One said to Subhūti: "For example, when various large and small streams have not yet entered the great ocean, they each have separate bases, the water differs, and the water increases or decreases.
Once they enter the great ocean, they have no separate bases; the water has no difference, and the water neither increases nor decreases."

In this way, as long as bodhisattvas have not yet entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, they have distinct bases of reliance, their wisdoms differ, and their wisdoms increase or decrease;

however, once they have entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, they have no distinct bases of reliance, their wisdoms are without difference, and their wisdoms neither increase nor decrease, as they experience the unified flavor of the wisdom of activities.
Bandhuprabha’s commentary states: Prior to one thousand years [after the Buddha's passing], the Buddha-dharma was of a single flavor;
after the passing of one thousand years, disputes arose between the proponents of Emptiness (śūnyatā) and Existence (astitva).

One thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, within the kingdom of Kañci in South India, two Bodhisattvas appeared simultaneously in the world: the first was Bhāviveka, and the second was Dharmapāla. In order to lead sentient beings to awaken to and enter the Buddha-dharma, they established the schools of Emptiness and Existence, thereby together fulfilling the Buddha’s intent.

The Bodhisattva Bhāviveka adhered to emptiness to negate existence, thereby causing the abandonment of the attachment to existence; the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla established existence to negate emptiness, thereby causing the abandonment of the attachment to emptiness.

Thus, emptiness does not contradict existence—the principle of emptiness is not non-existent—and the teaching that form is not distinct from emptiness establishes both emptiness and existence by itself. This accords with and perfects the Two Truths; being neither empty nor existent, it accords with the Middle Way. Is this not indeed the great core of the Buddha-dharma?
Question:
"How can the conflicting disputes over existence and non-existence possibly accord with the Buddha’s intention? Answer:
"To maintain the thesis that one is superior is a grave contradiction of the Holy Teaching.

The Buddha himself granted the status of a liberated Bodhisattva to [the other]; how much more so when two Bodhisattvas mutually influence one another to inspire understanding in sentient beings—would this contradict the Buddha's intention?"

Therefore, I shall now briefly describe two types of contemplative gateways (*vipaśyanā-mukha*). First, Bhāviveka, relying upon the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and the school of Nāgārjuna, establishes one contemplative gateway: the gateway of contemplating emptiness by sequentially eliminating characteristics through all phenomena. He posits that all phenomena are entirely empty, without arising or ceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning—one should contemplate them in this way.

Furthermore, the *Cintāmaṇi-cakra Sūtra* states: "To discriminate all phenomena with the mind is entirely erroneous; not to discriminate all phenomena with the mind is entirely correct. Moreover, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
"If there were anything that was not empty, then emptiness would have to exist. Since even 'non-emptiness' cannot be found, how much less can 'emptiness' be found?"

Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self, and at other times they speak of non-self; within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self."

There are numerous such scriptural passages as these that serve as authentic evidence. Therefore, Bhāviveka’s *Tattvāmṛtāvatāra* (The Jewel in the Palm) states: "Conditioned phenomena are empty in their true nature, because they arise dependently like illusions; unconditioned phenomena lack reality, for their non-arising is like flowers in the sky."

Second, regarding the protection of the Dharma, based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other texts, as well as the school of Maitreya, they establish a single gate of contemplation. This is the gate of contemplation that negates objects within consciousness to discern emptiness; it establishes that all phenomena are both existent and non-existent: the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is existent in terms of deluded cognition but non-existent in terms of principle; the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) exists due to causes and conditions; and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) exists in terms of principle and is not non-existent.
Therefore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states that it is based on the nature of what is grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that all phenomena are said to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states: "If one were to deny that all phenomena possess any nature at all, I declare such a person to be incurable.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state: "It is with reference to the nature of what is grasped that the sūtras teach that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature."

The verse from the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "False imagination exists; within it, these two [subject and object] are entirely absent. Within this, there is only emptiness, and within that, there is also this [false imagination]. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty, because of existence, non-existence, and the existence of both; thus, one accords with the Middle Way. There are indeed numerous such passages that serve as authentic proof.

Therefore, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts state: "One does not attain the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) by knowing that all phenomena are non-existent in every respect; rather, it is by realizing the absence of a self in the various phenomena that are the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) of fools that one is said to have entered into the selflessness of phenomena. Having presented the contemplation as above, I shall now explain the text.

Regarding the term "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*), they are namely: the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The five material sense faculties, their objects, and the matter included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) can be identified by spatial location and possess the characteristic of resistance; therefore, they are called "form."
Painful, pleasant, and neutral sensations are called "feeling" (*vedanā*) because they respectively experience disagreeable, agreeable, and intermediate objects.

Mental concomitants associated with all consciousnesses that grasp the boundaries of an object—such as male or female—are called "perception" (*saṃjñā*) because they give rise to various verbal designations.
Mental factors such as volition direct and mobilize the mind, causing it to perform wholesome and other actions; these are termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
The various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, discern their respective objects; therefore, they are termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
All five kinds possess the sense of accumulation; therefore, they are termed "aggregates" (*skandha*). These five aggregates are of three types:

first, the five aggregates of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), which exist in the mind but lack objective reality; second, the five aggregates of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), which exist as provisional designations based on causes and conditions; and third, the five aggregates of the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), which exist as ultimate reality according to the principle of truth.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga* states that there are three kinds of aggregates (*skandha*): first, the apprehended aggregate; second, the category aggregate; and third, the dharma-nature aggregate.
This refers to the new edition.

The *Eighteen Emptinesses Treatise* (*Aṣṭādaśaśūnyatā-śāstra*) likewise states this; thus that treatise says: "There are three kinds: first, conceptualization (*vikalpa*); second, categories (*prakāra*); and third, suchness (*tathatā*)."

Within each of these three types of five aggregates, there are both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena; the statement that they are "all empty" reveals the principle realized, which is precisely the aforementioned two types of emptiness.
Based on these various types of emptiness, two interpretations are distinguished. According to the school of Bhāviveka, there are two explanations:

first, that among the three natures, the first two are negated within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are explained as being empty.

Second, that all five aggregates (*skandha*) of the three natures are empty, as the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi* states: "The unconditioned has no reality; its non-arising is like a flower in the sky. By this standard, one should understand that the perfected nature is also negated.

According to the Dharmapāla school, among the three types of aggregates, one discerns emptiness solely by negating that which is grasped; the reasoning and scriptural authorities cited for this are as explained above.
Alternatively, some versions read, "He clearly perceives that the five aggregates, etc., are all empty. Although there are these two versions, the latter is the correct one.
Upon collating the Sanskrit manuscript, because the word "etc. (ādi) is present, the subsequent mention of "etc. should be understood accordingly.
As for "delivering all from suffering and calamity," this is the second [aspect] revealing the benefit for others.

This consists of three types: first, suffering itself is the calamity, hence it is called "suffering-calamity" (*duḥkha-āpad*); among the six types of compound analysis, this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. There is not a single contaminated phenomenon (*sāsrava-dharma*) that is not suffering;

therefore, the World-Honored One taught that the three realms are all suffering. However, this gate of suffering is briefly of three kinds, namely: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

In its intermediate sense, there are eight, namely: birth, old age, sickness, death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha-duḥkha*).

Extensively, there are the sufferings of suffering, which refer to the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*); as each of these possesses the four conditioned characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, they constitute one hundred sufferings.

The twenty-five states of existence consist of the four classes of beings, the four evil destinies, the four formless attainments, the four dhyānas, the Brahmā kings, the six heavens of the desire realm, the non-percipient beings, and the anāgāmins.

The first preliminary note states: Suffering and affliction are precisely the four afflictions—namely, desire (*kāma*), existence (*bhava*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and ignorance (*avidyā*). These four kinds bind all sentient beings and cause them to undergo various sufferings, just like a yoke.

If one follows this interpretation, it is called "suffering-impediment" (*duḥkha-vighāta*) because it is an impediment caused by suffering; thus, among the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaṭ-samāsa*), it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.

Alternatively, it may be said that "suffering" and "impediment" have distinct referents, as in the two previous interpretations; thus, among the six types of compound analysis, it is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound.
Regarding the phrase "Śāriputra," from this point downward is the second section, which distinguishes the object of contemplation.
This section contains two parts: first, the distinction of emptiness by means of the four propositions; second, the manifestation of the characteristics of emptiness based on six meanings.
The preceding section has two parts: first, the designation of those who receive the teaching; second, the formal exposition of emptiness. This [passage] is the designation of the person.
In the Sanskrit language, his name is Śāriputra, or alternatively Śāradvatīputra. Here, "Śāri" is translated as "mynah," and "putra" means "son."

Because his mother’s eyes were as blue and clear as those of a magpie, she was given the name "Magpie" (*śārikā*); thus he was styled *Śāriputra* (Son of the Magpie) in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, or *Gṛdhra-kūṭa-putra* (Son of the Vulture Peak). Alternatively, he is called *Upatiṣya*, which is a name derived from his father. The old translation "Son of the Body" (*Shenzi*) is erroneous.
Question:
"This prajñāpāramitā is the dharma of bodhisattvas; why did the World-Honored One address it to Śāriputra rather than to a bodhisattva? Answer:

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Śāriputra attained ten thousand samādhis and was foremost in wisdom among all the Buddha’s disciples; therefore, the World-Honored One declared that if one were to compare the wisdom and erudition of all sentient beings—excluding only the Buddha, the World-Honored One—to that of Śāriputra, they would not equal even a single sixteenth part of it.

Furthermore, Śāriputra was only eight years old when he established his arguments; his words and principles were so transcendent that all masters of debate marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, and everyone—whether foolish or wise, great or small—was subdued.

The remaining causes and conditions are as extensively explained in that treatise; therefore, it is here addressed to Śāriputra, with the further intent of leading those of the Lesser Vehicle to turn toward the Mahāyāna.

As for the statement, "Form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, emptiness is itself form," this correctly elucidates the nature of emptiness by means of the four propositions.

Within this, there are two parts: first, distinguishing four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) based on the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha); second, showing that the other four aggregates likewise each possess four alternatives. This [section] distinguishes the four alternatives based on the aggregate of form.

In order to explain the four propositions, one first distinguishes the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As previously analyzed, there are two kinds of emptiness: first, the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and second, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) that has been explained is of four kinds. First, the non-existence of the grasped self is called emptiness, because it is not included among the categories of phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, in the "Bodhisattvabhūmi," states: "Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are termed 'existent'; the absence of self and what belongs to self is termed 'non-existent'."
Second, the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); because it is that which is elucidated by emptiness, it is also called "empty.

Third, the specific emptiness of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors subsumed under the Truth of Suffering; since it takes the contaminated five aggregates as its essence, the sixth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The specific emptiness is not-self, because it belongs to the Truth of Suffering."

Fourth, all phenomena (dharmas) are encompassed by universal emptiness and non-self; since they take these very phenomena as their essential nature, the various sūtras state that all phenomena are without self.

Although there are four kinds [of emptiness], based on the principle of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), they are subsumed into three: first, the emptiness of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*); second, the emptiness of the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*); and third, the emptiness of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*). These take the three natures as their respective essences in that order.
Regarding the four types of emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), although there is no explicit textual authority, when examined through reasoning, they should comprise four categories.

The three types of emptiness of phenomena should be understood by analogy with the above. If analyzed extensively, there are eighteen kinds of emptiness, as in the *Aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā-śāstra*; according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, some speak of sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, or even twenty types, as fully detailed in that sūtra.

Now, relying on the three natures (trisvabhāva), I shall explain these four propositions. Among these four propositions, the first two state the fundamental tenets and provide the correct exposition, while the latter two dispel the doubts of external opponents.
"Form is not different from emptiness" indicates that the conventional is not different from the ultimate;
"emptiness is not different from form" indicates that the ultimate is not different from the conventional.
The latter part dispels external doubts, for an externalist might raise this doubt:
"Is it because they depend upon one another that they are not different?
Or is it because they are identical in nature that they are called not different?

Therefore, this was said: "Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. It is not because they depend upon one another that they are called not different, nor is it because they are identical in nature that they are called not different.
Based on this very text, the masters of the West have two interpretations of their own. First, Bhāviveka and others say:

"Form has three kinds, namely the imagined and so forth; emptiness is that which dispels their nature, yet its essence is not the three natures. When it is now said that 'form is itself emptiness,' it means that because the thoroughly imagined nature is fundamentally non-existent, it is described as empty."

In reality, even this emptiness is not empty; thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If there were a non-empty phenomenon, then there would have to be an empty phenomenon. Since in truth there is no non-empty phenomenon, how could there be an empty phenomenon?"
The emptiness of the latter two natures should be understood by analogy with this. The statement that they are "empty" is taught in order to eliminate the grasping at existence.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is empty because it arises from conditions, being like an illusion and so forth.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is empty of its own essence as well, for it does not arise and is thus like a flower in the sky.

Within the interpretation of this school, there is another explanation: it is commonly accepted by both schools that the former two natures are not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because they are free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and transcend all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Question:
"Are form and emptiness one or different?
If they were of one essence and identical in nature, it would constitute the attachment to oneness."
If their substance were different, that would be the adherence to difference;
if they were both one and different, how could they not be contradictory?
If they were neither one nor different, it would result in mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
To explain these four propositions, they are differentiated into two interpretations.

First, non-Buddhists and those of the Hīnayāna mostly rely on the gate of manifestation (*vyañjana*) when speaking of the four propositions, such as existence and non-existence, because there is something being signified (*abhidheya*).

Second, according to the Mahāyāna, all statements concerning existence, non-existence, and so forth are exclusively apophatic (paryudāsa-pratiṣedha), because all phenomena are inexpressible. Nevertheless, all phenomena possess two characteristics, namely the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa). The particular characteristic is apprehended solely by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for it cannot be apprehended by conceptual cognition or verbal expression.
If that which is apprehended by conceptual cognition (*kalpanā*) and verbal expression is what is being discussed, it refers to the "universal" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

For example, when one speaks of "blue," the characteristics of the stalk, leaves, and so forth are each distinct and are apprehended solely through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Consequently, conceptual cognition and various verbal expressions can only express the universal of "blue. When one says "blue," because it excludes yellow and other colors, it is called "expressing blue"; however, this does not directly express the blue itself. Therefore, it is called "exclusionary expression" (*paryudāsa*).

Within the context of negation (*paryudāsa*), there are two positions. First is the school of Bhāviveka: its ontological principle cannot be designated by names nor characterized by marks; it negates without clinging and establishes without affirmation. The principles and scriptures cited therein should be understood according to the above.

Second, the Dharma-protecting school maintains that both conventional and ultimate principles exist as real entities and are all beyond verbal expression. Within this context, the term "true nature" is employed in contrast to the conventional; it is not the case that there is nothing to be signified.
Within the school of Bhāviveka, the explanation given by one master is also identical to this.

Therefore, Dharmapāla refutes Bhāviveka, saying: "If one asserts that all phenomena are empty based on ultimate reality (tattva), it results in the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana)."

Regarding the distinction between the systems of Bhāviveka and Dharmapāla: because Bhāviveka negates the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) while Dharmapāla does not permit it, there is a difference between them.

By this principle, all statements concerning existence, non-existence, and so forth within our own school (*svayūthya*) are exclusively *paryudāsa-pratiṣedha* (implicative negation), thereby avoiding the faults of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) such as identity and difference.
The explanation of the text according to the school of Bhāviveka is hereby completed.
Second, regarding the four propositions according to the school of Dharmapāla: form is of three kinds, namely, form as the three natures;
emptiness is likewise of three kinds, its essence being the three natures.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga states in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*: "Emptiness is of three kinds: first, emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), because its nature is not existent;
second, emptiness of other-nature (*anya-bhāva-śūnyatā*), because it is different from the intrinsic nature falsely grasped by delusion;
third, emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), because that which is revealed by these two [other] emptinesses constitutes its own nature."

Based on the four propositions concerning imagined form (*parikalpita-rūpa*) in relation to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there are three types. First, the four propositions are distinguished by contrasting imagined form with imagined emptiness: the forms such as the sense faculties and their objects, as conceived according to worldly attachment, are not different from the originally non-existent emptiness of what is imagined; therefore, it is said that "form is itself emptiness. Since the originally non-existent emptiness appears as existent according to worldly attachment, it is said that "emptiness is itself form. This is the mutual identity based on sameness of nature (*sabhāgatva*).
The two phrases indicating the fundamental tenet should be understood according to the above.

Second, the four alternatives are distinguished by contrasting the grasped form (*parikalpita-rūpa*) with the emptiness of the dependent nature (*paratantra-śūnyatā*): because the grasped form, which is superposed upon the dependent nature, is not different from the emptiness of the dependent nature’s lack of reality, it is said that "form is itself emptiness"; yet because that deluded mind clings to the presence of real form within that state of emptiness, it is said that "emptiness is itself form."
The two phrases indicating the thesis can be understood by analogy.
This refers to the mutual identity of different natures (*anyatva*).

Third, regarding the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) established by contrasting the grasped form (*grāhya-rūpa*) with the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): one clings to the perfected nature as being real form that is not distinct from the emptiness of its own nature; and one clings to the emptiness of its own nature as being real form. Therefore, it is said that "form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form."
The two phrases indicating the thesis can be understood by analogy.
This is like the mutual identity of different entities within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*):

when the form of the dependent nature is contrasted with the emptiness of other-nature (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*), there are four propositions. Namely, the form produced by conditions is not different from the emptiness of other-nature; yet, because this nature of emptiness possesses substantial resistance (*sapratigha*), it is said that "form is itself emptiness" and "emptiness is itself form. This constitutes the mutual identity of identical natures (*sabhāva*).
The two phrases indicating the central thesis should be understood according to the same principle.

Furthermore, regarding the fourfold tetralemma concerning the emptiness of the two natures in contrast to form produced through other-dependent origination, because it concerns a different nature, it does not differ from the previous explanation. Regarding the fourfold tetralemma in contrast to the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), it is as follows: the functional activity of dependently originated form takes [emptiness] as its essence; yet that emptiness is not distinct from the other-dependent nature.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Thus, this [perfected nature] and the dependent nature are neither different nor non-different, just like the nature of impermanence and so forth."

Furthermore, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "In this [dependent nature], there is only emptiness; in that [emptiness], there is also this [dependent nature]. By this principle, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) are mutually inseparable; therefore, it is said that form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.

Because emptiness is not produced through conditions, it is said that their characteristics are identical; otherwise, one would incur the fault of contradicting the fundamental tenet. This is an identity of distinct natures.
The two phrases stating the thesis should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) in relation to the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), there are four propositions: namely, that the perfected nature is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); because it is the true nature of form, it is designated as "form";
and because it is revealed by the twofold emptiness of self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), it is called the "emptiness of the perfected.
By this principle, it is said that "form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form"; this is the mutual identity of the same nature (*tulya-jāti*).
The two phrases indicating the central thesis should be understood accordingly.

As for the statement, "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this," this constitutes the second category of explanation regarding the four aggregates (*skandhas*). Each aggregate possesses four phrases, and these four phrases are mutually identical; this should be understood by analogy with what was stated above.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: this sutra exists in two versions. One version is as presented above;

the other version of the sutra states, "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Regarding the term "etcetera" (*ādi*), according to the subsequent text of the sutra, there are six skillful means (*kauśalya*), namely: the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the four truths (*catuḥsatya*), enlightenment (*bodhi*), and nirvana. Here, by citing the four aggregates and so forth, it indicates that the remaining five categories all possess four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*); therefore, the word "etcetera" is used.
The distinctions among the meanings of the six gates shall be analyzed later.

"Śāriputra, this mark of emptiness of all dharmas is neither born nor extinguished; it is neither defiled nor pure; it neither increases nor decreases"—from here on, the second section clarifies the mark of emptiness by means of six types of meaning.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the correct elucidation of the characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by means of six meanings; second, the elimination of the dharmas of the six gates based on those characteristics of emptiness.

Regarding the elucidation of these six characteristics, Śāriputra was addressed as explained above; these six characteristics are precisely non-arising, non-ceasing, non-defilement, non-purity, non-increase, and non-decrease.
Regarding these six characteristics, there are two interpretations in the West: first, that of Bhāviveka, and second, that of Dharmapāla.

According to the school of Bhāviveka, the explanation of the six characteristics is as follows: that which was non-existent now exists is called "arising"; that which was temporarily existent returns to non-existence is called "cessation," as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. That which is by nature defiled and impure is called "defilement" (*mala*); being free from defilement and not impure is termed "purity," as taught in various scriptures. To assert that phenomena possess functional utility is called "increase"; the false conceptualization of the destruction of phenomena is called "decrease," as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Regarding the three pairs of six characteristics, there are three different explanations.

The first states that this text distinguishes the three based on stages: because the nature of true emptiness is free from all characteristics, prior to the path one is far removed from the arising and ceasing of transmigration; during the path, there is neither delusion nor wisdom, neither defilement nor purity; and after the path, one eternally abandons the increase or decrease of essence and function.

First, this text distinguishes the three [natures] based on their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*): because the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) has been non-existent from the beginning, it is neither born nor extinguished; because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises from conditions, it is neither defiled nor pure; and because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) does not arise, it neither increases nor decreases.
First, this discourse presents three pairs of six aspects; each one universally applies to all stages and all natures, collectively dispelling the three natures because nothing remains.
Among these three, the latter is superior because it accords with our own school’s tenets.

According to the system of Dharmapāla, in reality the characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) are manifold—namely, neither identical nor different, neither existent nor non-existent, and so forth. However, the Sūtra mentions only three pairs, totaling six, for the following reasons: arising and ceasing refer to the general characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); defilement and purity distinguish the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of various phenomena; and increase and decrease express the functional efficacy (*artha-kriyā*) inherent in phenomena.

In reality, the three types of emptiness all encompass six characteristics; however, the intent of the sutra is precisely to reveal that this is the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), because the true principle revealed by the two types of emptiness—emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*) and emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—serves as the basis for both delusion and enlightenment.

Regarding the passage, "Therefore, in emptiness there is no form; no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," this is the second section below, which relies on the previously established characteristics of emptiness to dispel the dharmas of the six gates.

The method of dispelling through the six gates is divided into six parts; this is the first, the gate of dispelling the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). It means that all phenomena are empty and possess six characteristics; therefore, within emptiness, there are no phenomena of the five aggregates.

The meanings of the five aggregates have already been explained as before. The six categories of phenomena taught herein collectively manifest the two types of objects—general and specific—of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Because the first three primarily reveal the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are said to be the general objects of the three vehicles.
Based upon that very nature of phenomena, the subsequent doors such as dependent origination are taught according to individual faculties; therefore, the latter three are called the specific objects.

Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra states: "For the sake of śrāvakas, he preaches the Dharma of the Four Truths; for the sake of pratyekabuddhas, he preaches the Dharma of dependent origination; and for the sake of all bodhisattvas, he preaches the Dharma of the Six Perfections."

The statement, "There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there is no form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomenon," refers to the second [stage], which eliminates the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Now, the meaning of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) will be briefly explained through a threefold analysis:
first, clarifying the arising of the teaching; second, explaining the names; and third, identifying their essential natures (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the emergence of the verbal teachings, there are inherently two intentions, namely: the realization and entry into the two kinds of emptiness—of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

As for entering the emptiness of persons, it is as stated in that *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "Based on these teachings concerning the twelve bases (*āyatana*), if one understands that the six consciousnesses arise from the six pairs of factors, and that there is absolutely no seer up to no knower, one is then able to realize the selflessness of sentient beings."

Regarding "entering the emptiness of phenomena" (*dharmāśūnyatā*): this refers to what has been explained above—the refutation of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) to reveal the principle of the emptiness of phenomena.
The differences in their methods of refuting phenomena between Bhāviveka and Dharmapāla should be reflected upon as described above.
Next, regarding the explanation of the names, there is first the general and then the specific.

First, the general clarification of the twelve bases (*āyatana*): "twelve" indicates the number; "base" (*āyatana*) has the meaning of "growth and production. This means that because the six sense faculties and their objects produce and grow all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), they are called "bases. Among the six types of grammatical analysis, this is an analysis by enumeration (*saṃkhyā-vigraha*).

Regarding the subsequent specific names, as stated in the third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "Furthermore, because one repeatedly contemplates various forms and, having contemplated them, lets them go, it is therefore called the 'eye'."
Because it repeatedly reaches and is able to hear these sounds, it is called the ear (*śrotra*).
Because one repeatedly smells various fragrances by means of this, it is called the nose (*ghrāṇa*).
Because it can remove hunger and weakness, repeatedly produce speech, and manifest through calling and summoning, it is called the tongue (*jihvā*).
Because it is that which is followed by the various faculties and is accumulated throughout its entirety, it is called the "body" (*kāya*).
For a long night, the foolish person polishes, adorns, and guards it, grasping at it as "mine," reckoning it as "I" and "myself."

Furthermore, the various worldly conventions rely upon this to establish diverse designations and concepts, such as "sentient being," "person," "life-principle," "born one," "mind-born," and "youth"; therefore, it is called "mind" (*manas*).
It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because its numerical instances can be manifested, and because it possesses substantial resistance that can increase within its spatial location.
It is called "sound" (*śabda*) because its numerical instances are subject to frequent arising and ceasing, and because they follow an increase in diverse discourses.
It leaves its substance and conceals its form, frequently shifting with the wind; therefore, it is called "fragrance" (gandha).
It can be tasted by the tongue, yet it frequently brings about illness and suffering; therefore, it is called "taste" (rasa).
"Numbers can be realized by the body; therefore, they are called 'contact' (spraṣṭavya).
They are able to sustain [the body] everywhere, and their nature is solely that which is remembered by the mind; therefore, they are called 'phenomena' (dharma)."

Third, regarding the essential nature [of the sense organs]: as explained in various treatises, the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), serves as the basis for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and has translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) as its essence.

As with the eye faculty, so it is for the ear faculty (*śrotrendriya*) up to the other faculties: they are composed of the four great elements, serve as the bases for their respective auditory consciousnesses (*śrotravijñāna*), and have translucent matter as their essence.
The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) takes all eight consciousnesses as its substance.

As for "form" (*rūpa*), as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is derived from the four great elements, is the object of the visual faculty, and has twenty-five types of color as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). These are: blue, yellow, red, white; long, short, square, round; coarse, fine, high, low; even, uneven; light, shadow, brightness, darkness; clouds, smoke, dust, mist; the color of the distant horizon; manifesting color; and the color of space.

Sound is of eleven kinds: namely, that which is agreeable, that which is disagreeable, that which is neither, that which arises from primary elements associated with feeling, that which arises from primary elements not associated with feeling, that which arises from both types of primary elements, that which is conventionally established, that which is derived, that which is conceptually constructed, that which is included within noble speech, and that which is not included within noble speech.
There are six kinds of fragrance: namely, pleasant fragrance, unpleasant fragrance, neutral fragrance, innate fragrance, blended fragrance, and transformed fragrance.
There are twelve kinds of taste: bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, bland, agreeable, disagreeable, neutral, innate, blended, and transformed.

There are twenty-six types of tangibles, namely: the four great elements; smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, softness, slackness, tension, cold, hunger, thirst, turbidity, satiety, strength, weakness, oppression, itching, stickiness, illness, old age, death, fatigue, respiration, and vigor.

These five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are explained in detail in the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*; the similarities and differences regarding various treatises are fully detailed in a separate chapter.

The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) takes eighty-two dharmas from among the hundred dharmas as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): namely, fifty-one among the mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*), one among form (*rūpa*), which is the form included in the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), and thirty among the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
There are twenty-four dissociated [factors] and six unconditioned [factors].

According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises, these consist of eighty-eight factors as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), namely: the four types of form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) and the two unconditioned [factors], as explained in detail therein.
The detailed analysis of other categories is as extensive as in the separate chapter.
The phrase "There is no eye-element, up to and including no consciousness-element" refers to the third negation of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

These eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are analyzed through three gates: first, the manifestation of the teaching; second, the explanation of their names; and third, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the manifestation of the teaching: it is for those who cling to form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as a self (*ātman*), as well as those of inferior faculties, that the World-Honored One taught the eighteen elements.
Next, regarding the explanation of the names, there is first the general and then the specific.

As for the general name "eighteen realms" (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), "eighteen" is the number, and "realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*) as well as "distinct nature" (*prakāra*). Because all phenomena consist of eighteen lineages and distinct natures, this is an analytical compound expressing a number (*saṃkhyā-vīpsā-vyākhyāna*); this should be understood according to the previous explanation.
Next, regarding the specific names: the six faculties and six objects are as explained in the section on the bases (*āyatana*). As for the naming of the six consciousnesses, there are two meanings.

First, they are named according to their objects, ranging from "consciousness of form" (*rūpa-vijñāna*) to "consciousness of phenomena" (*dharma-vijñāna*); these names are established in accordance with the objects because it accords with the meaning of "consciousness."

Second, they are named after their respective faculties, ranging from "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) up to "mind-consciousness" (*manovijñāna*). These names are established according to the faculties because they possess five meanings, such as "subduing" (*ava-sthāpana*) and "arising" (*utpādana*).

Since it is the consciousness of form, it is called "form-consciousness" (*rūpavijñāna*); likewise, since it is the consciousness of mind, it is called "mind-consciousness" (*manovijñāna*). Therefore, among the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*), this is an *upapada-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
If one were to provide a detailed analysis, it is as explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Regarding the subsequent clarification of their essential nature: the twelve bases, such as the eye and so forth, are as described in the section on the *āyatanas*; as for the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, within the system of the hundred dharmas, they take the six consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and the rest—as their intrinsic nature according to their respective names.
The remaining sections are as extensively detailed in various treatises.

The passage, "There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death," constitutes the fourth gate, which dispels [the notion of] dependent origination.
However, this dependent origination itself is of two kinds: first, the process of flow (pravṭtti), and second, the process of cessation (nivṛtti).

Due to ignorance, the various formations (saṃskāra) arise; continuing thus until, with birth as a condition, there is old age and death. In this manner, the forward flow through the five destinies and four modes of birth is like the full moon disk, the beginning of which cannot be known.
Within emptiness, there is no such cyclic flow; therefore, the Sūtra says: "There is no ignorance, up to and including no old age and death.

Through the power of insight, ignorance is extinguished; because ignorance is extinguished, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are also extinguished, and so on until, through the extinction of birth, old age and death are also extinguished. This is the wheel turning back toward *nirvāṇa*, and is thus called "reversion" (*pratiloma*).
Within emptiness, there is no such cessation; therefore, the Sūtra also says: "There is no exhaustion of ignorance, up to and including no exhaustion of old age and death.

As for how this sūtra is taught from the perspective of the gate of origination: just as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* teaches dependent origination for the sake of those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, whereas here this gate of dependent origination is taught in order to reveal the emptiness of phenomena.
However, this dependent origination differs from conventional explanations; therefore, I shall now briefly analyze it through three sections:
first, the explanation of the name; second, the determination of its essence; and third, the establishment and exclusion of its categories.
Regarding the explanation of the definition, there is first the general and then the specific.

As for the general definition, "twelve" is the general indication of the number; as stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, these various members each arise through the continuous succession of their respective conditions in a complete and unimpeded manner, and are therefore called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the cause is termed "conditioned awakening" (*pratyaya-bodha*) and the fruit is termed "conditioned arising" (*pratyaya-jāti*).

Within this name, the number is cited to manifest the essential doctrine; therefore, among the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*), this is an analytical compound denoting a number (*dvigu*).
As for the subsequent mention of its specific name: because it is ignorance regarding the three time periods and lacks comprehension of objects, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
The three types of karma, such as merit and so forth, which involve flux and volitional construction, are termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
The eight consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and others, which discern their respective objects, are termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Form and so forth, which denote material obstruction, are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
The six sense bases, such as the eye and so forth, which cause the growth of the mind and its associates, are named the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The three types of contact, such as that of suffering, are called "contact" because they encounter their respective objects.
The three types of feeling, such as that of suffering, are called "feeling" because they experience what is favorable, unfavorable, and so forth.
Craving for one's own self and so on is called "craving" because it defiles its own object.
The four types of grasping, such as the grasping for sensual pleasures, which cling to objects and so forth, are called "grasping" (*upādāna*).
The seeds of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth, which are capable of producing birth and the rest, are therefore called "existence" (*bhava*).
That these five factors, beginning with consciousness, which were originally non-existent, now come into being, is called birth.
That those same five factors undergo decay, transformation, and disintegration is called old age and death.

The second [section], the determination of the substance (*svabhāva*), has three meanings: first, the differentiation of what is produced; second, the emergence of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and third, the distinction between the manifest and the seeds (*bīja*).

Regarding the distinction of projection (*ākṣepa*): ignorance (*avidyā*) and formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are called the "projectors" because they project the seeds of the five results, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Consciousness and the other four [results] are called the "projected" because they are brought forth by those two preceding members.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are called "the producers," because they directly produce future birth, aging, and death;
whereas birth and aging-and-death are "the produced," because they are what is directly produced by craving, grasping, and existence.

To clarify the essential nature [of the members]: the capacity to initiate the three types of karma—meritorious, non-meritorious, and neutral—is the member of ignorance (*avidyā*). That which is initiated by it constitutes the essence of the member of formative forces (*saṃskāra*). That which directly produces the seeds of the eighth consciousness in the future constitutes the essence of the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Excluding the last three causes, all other causes constitute the essence of the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The last three causes correspond to the sequence of names, namely the latter three types [of causes].

There is an interpretation that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) comprises five types as its intrinsic nature; among these, the others are established according to their predominance. Specifically, the seed of the *ālayavijñāna* is termed the limb of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*). The other three [limbs]—the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth—are established as being able to moisten the seeds of the six [karmic] formations (*saṃskāra*). Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is defined as desire. Based on craving, the further arising of the four types of grasping, such as sensual desire, constitutes the essence of the limb of grasping (*upādānāṅga*). However, regarding these four types of grasping, as stated in the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, they constitute the essence of the limb of grasping in their respective order: namely, the desire arising toward the objects of sensual pleasure, the other four views, improper conduct, and the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the similarities and differences between the Sūtras and the Śāstras, as in the case of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and so forth: once the six kinds of seeds—such as formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—have been moistened, they are subsequently designated as "existence" (*bhava*). The resultant phenomena produced by these five factors, from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) through the stage in the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) prior to decay and transformation, are termed the "limb of birth" (*jāti*). When they reach the stage of decay and transformation, it is collectively termed "aging" (*jarā*), and the dissolution of the body and end of life is called "death" (*maraṇa*).

Regarding the distinction between the manifest (*pratyutpanna*) and the seeds (*bīja*), there are two senses: first, from the perspective of the ultimate correct principle; second, from the perspective of figurative designation based on conformity.

In the sense of figurative designation, each [link] encompasses both the seed and the manifest state; therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* states that ignorance has two aspects: first, the causal link (*hetu-aṅga*), and second, the resultant link (*phala-aṅga*). It should be understood that this applies likewise up to old age and death.

According to the correct principle of ultimate reality, birth and old age and death are only manifest and not seeds; the six branches beginning with consciousness are only seeds and not manifest; while ignorance, formations, craving, and grasping all pertain to both the manifest and the seeds.

The third section, concerning the establishment and abolition [of the factors], has three meanings: first, the general establishment and abolition of all factors; second, the analysis of the factors through their expansion and contraction; and third, the discernment of their similarities and differences according to the time periods and stages.
Regarding the establishment or abolition of the links [of dependent origination], it is as stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
Question:
"Why is the stage of old age not established as a separate link?"
Answer: "Because they do not necessarily exist [in every case], the factors are established in relation to death.
Question:
"Why is illness not a factor?
Answer: "Because it is neither pervasive nor fixed."

"Although old age is not universal, it is established as a link because it is pervasive; for in all realms, destinies, and births—excluding those who die prematurely—all who are about to end their lives possess the process of decay.
Question:
"Since name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is not universal, why is it established as a link?"
Answer: "The factors are established on the basis of certainty.
In the cases of birth from a womb, egg, or moisture, as long as the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not yet complete, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is certain."

Furthermore, the factors of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) are also universally present; for although those born by transformation in the realm of form possess the five sense faculties at the initial moment of conception, they do not yet function, and thus at that time they are not yet designated as the factor of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).

Likewise, although those newly born in the formless realm certainly possess the mental faculty (manas), it is not yet distinct, and thus it is not yet designated as the sense base of mind (manāyatana).
Question:
"Craving is not universally present; why then establish it as a separate link?
For those born in the miserable realms do not crave them."
Answer: "It is established separately because it is fixed.
Those who seek not non-existence but are born in the happy realms possess fixed craving."
Question:
"If that is so, would it not follow that the Non-returner (anāgāmin) has no craving? Answer:
"Although it does not manifest [at that time], it must certainly exist as a seed, just as it was grasped previously.

Furthermore, craving is pervasive; even those born in the miserable realms possess craving for the objects of their present 'self. Thus, it is based on this craving for a body in the miserable realms, rather than on a desire for them."
The Sūtra states that they do not exist, yet this does not mean they are entirely non-existent.

Regarding the distinctions between opening and closing, there are two meanings: first, distinguishing opening and closing through the relationship between leading and generating; second, distinguishing opening and closing through the relationship between activating and moistening.

The relationship between the projecting [causes] and the projected [results] is as explained in that treatise. For what reason are "birth" (*jāti*) and "aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇa*) established for the projected results, while the projecting causes are separately established as the five branches beginning with "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)?

Because the specific characteristics of the causal stage are difficult to discern, the five branches are separately established based on the perspective of the future resultant stage; this is explained in full detail therein.

Because the characteristics of the distinctions between the stages of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) are easy to understand, two factors are established in total to manifest the three types of suffering, as explained in detail therein.
The distinction between "arousing" (*utpādana*) and "moistening" (*sneha*) is as stated in that treatise.
For what reason is ignorance established as the general factor for initiating karma, while craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are established separately within the stage of moistening karma?

Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of both initiating and moistening karma, the power of ignorance is predominant; it is fully present there as well, yet at the stage of initiating karma, the power of ignorance increases because it possesses eleven superior factors—namely, its object (*ālambana*) and so forth—as explained at length in the Sūtra.

In the stage of moistening karma, the power of craving increases preeminently; craving is said to be like water because it can irrigate and moisten, and only through repeated watering does the sprout of existence arise.
Furthermore, based on the first and last [limbs], craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are distinguished as two;
because there is no sense of repeated arising, ignorance (*avidyā*) is established as one.

Thirdly, regarding the distinction between their similarities and differences across time-periods (*adhvan*) and stages (*bhūmi*), there are two points: first, distinguishing similarities and differences by way of stages; second, distinguishing similarities and differences by way of time-periods.

Regarding the identity and difference of levels (*bhūmi*), as stated in that treatise: all members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) proceed by depending upon their own respective level. However, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of a higher level may be produced by depending on the ignorance (*avidyā*) of a lower level, just as the ignorance of a lower level produces the formative forces of a higher level. Were it not so, the higher meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) first attained by subduing the defilements of a lower level would not constitute the member of "formative forces," because the ignorance of that [higher] level has not yet arisen.

Regarding "belonging to the same or different lifetimes," as stated in that treatise: these twelve links consist of ten causes and two results, which are definitely not of the same lifetime; among the causes, the first seven may either be of a different lifetime or the same lifetime as craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).

If two, three, or seven [links] were each fixed to the same time period, then these twelve links in a single causal sequence would suffice to manifest cyclic existence and to exclude the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; establishing two such sequences would indeed be redundant, or else one would have to exceed this number, leading to an infinite regress.

The commentary states: This treatise first presents its own school’s single-layered dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and refutes the two-layered dependent origination of the Sarvāstivādins; this can be understood by following the text.
The remaining various sections are explained extensively as they appear therein.
"Neither suffering, nor its origin, nor its cessation, nor the path"—this is the fifth gate of dispelling the Four Noble Truths.

As for how this gate of the Four Noble Truths is explained: as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the four truths were taught for those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvakas; whereas in this present sutra, in order to reveal the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths are dispelled.

Now, these Four Noble Truths are analyzed through three gates: first, the explanation of their names; second, the determination of their essential nature; and third, the distinctions among their categories.
Regarding the explanation of the names, we shall proceed first with the general and then with the specific.

Regarding the general designation: "four" indicates the number; "truth" (*satya*) has two meanings, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: first, the meaning of being inseparable from the characteristics as they have been described; second, the sense of reaching the ultimate state by virtue of being free from these [defilements].
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound), which may be understood according to the preceding explanation.

Regarding the specific names: as the truths are distinct and not identical, there are four types: first, suffering (*duḥkha*); second, origination (*samudaya*); third, cessation (*nirodha*); and fourth, the path (*mārga*).

That which is designated as suffering because it consists of the three types of suffering is called *duḥkha*; that which is able to summon future results is called *samudaya* (the origin); that which is the exhaustion of both origin and suffering is called *nirodha* (cessation); and that which is able to eliminate [suffering] and lead to penetration is called *mārga* (the path).

Second, regarding the determination of their essential nature: the Truth of Suffering consists of the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*); that which produces afflictions and karma constitutes the Truth of Origination; the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the essence of the Truth of Cessation; and the Truth of the Path consists of the uncontaminated noble path (*āryamārga*).
Regarding the third classification by number, there are either two or three.
As for the two: first, the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and second, the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Within each of these truths, all four truths are fully present; as explained in works such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, I shall not elaborate here for fear of prolixity.
According to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, there are also two kinds: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
